accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD 19) with treated HCC — precipitated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (ascitic PMN 310/mm³) plus rifaximin non-adherence and recent alcohol use.

differential.diagnosis: Septic encephalopathy from SBP (primary precipitant rather than separate diagnosis)
differential.key_features: Ascitic PMN 310/mm³ confirms SBP; cytokine-driven hyperammonemia and reduced hepatic clearance both contribute — treat as HE precipitated by SBP rather than 'septic encephalopathy' alone.
Ethanol 14 mg/dL is too low to drive grade III obtundation in a tolerant alcoholic; withdrawal risk exists 48-72 h post-stop and warrants monitoring with non-benzodiazepine first-line measures.
Coagulopathy (INR 2.2) + thrombocytopenia raise risk; non-contrast CT head excludes hemorrhage.
Chronic alcohol use places patient at risk; no ophthalmoplegia / classic triad; give empiric thiamine before dextrose regardless.
Solitary 1.8 cm post-TACE HCC; no focal deficits; MRI would assess if clinical course atypical.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Infection (especially SBP) is the single most common HE precipitant in decompensated cirrhotics with ascites; diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory.
Rifaximin non-adherence is an under-recognized but very common precipitant of overt HE in patients on secondary prophylaxis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ethanol at 14 mg/dL cannot cause grade III HE in a tolerant alcoholic; ammonia 88 + ascitic PMN 310 = HE precipitated by SBP.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute grade III obtundation to acute alcohol intoxication and adopt 'wait it out' management.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Solitary post-TACE HCC and no focal deficits make CNS metastasis very unlikely; treat HE with SBP precipitant first; MRI only if clinical course atypical.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue HCC progression / brain metastasis workup as primary cause of AMS.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. B. is a 61-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C), prior HCC treated with TACE, and a prior HE episode 4 months ago now on rifaximin prophylaxis, brought by his daughter for acute confusion and agitation over the preceding 24 hours. His daughter reported he was found disoriented in the bathroom at 2 AM, had been slurring his speech since yesterday evening, and had been combative and uncooperative throughout the morning. She found an empty vodka bottle in his room, and he admitted on direct questioning to having drunk 'a little yesterday.' His serum ethanol level on arrival was 14 mg/dL — a low but detectable level. He had last been seen by hepatology 3 weeks ago when labs showed stable MELD 18. Over the prior week, his daughter noticed decreasing oral intake, reduced rifaximin adherence (ran out 5 days ago and had not refilled), and increasing abdominal distension. He denied hematemesis or melena. Temperature on arrival was 37.9°C.
